## Data

The data comes from the
[Iris dataset included in scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.datasets.load_iris.html).

The dataset contains measurements of 150 iris flowers from three species:
Setosa, Versicolor, and Virginica.

## Load and inspect the data

```{python}
#| echo: true

from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

iris = load_iris(as_frame=True)
df = iris.frame

df["species"] = df["target"].map(
    dict(enumerate(iris.target_names))
)

df.head()
```

The dataset contains measurements of sepal length, sepal width, petal
length, and petal width. I also created a `species` column so that the
three flower species are easier to interpret than the numerical target
values.

## Average measurements by species

```{python}
#| echo: true

df.groupby("species")[
    [
        "sepal length (cm)",
        "sepal width (cm)",
        "petal length (cm)",
        "petal width (cm)"
    ]
].mean()
```

The average measurements differ across the three species. Setosa flowers
have substantially shorter and narrower petals, while Virginica flowers
generally have the largest petal measurements.

## Petal length distribution by species

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-petal-boxplot
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of petal length for each Iris species."

df.boxplot(
    column="petal length (cm)",
    by="species"
)

plt.xlabel("Species")
plt.ylabel("Petal length (cm)")
plt.title("Petal Length by Species")
plt.suptitle("")
plt.show()
```

The box plot shows clear differences in petal length among the three
species. Setosa has much shorter petals, while Virginica generally has
the longest petals.

## Correlation between flower measurements

Next, I examined how strongly the four numerical flower measurements are
related to one another.

```{python}
#| echo: true

measurement_columns = [
    "sepal length (cm)",
    "sepal width (cm)",
    "petal length (cm)",
    "petal width (cm)"
]

correlations = df[measurement_columns].corr()

correlations.round(2)
```

Petal length and petal width have a strong positive relationship. Sepal
length also tends to increase as petal length and petal width increase.
Sepal width shows a different pattern and has weaker relationships with
some of the other measurements.

## Number of flowers by species

Finally, I checked whether all three species have the same number of
observations in the dataset.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-species-count
#| fig-cap: "Number of Iris observations for each species."

species_counts = df["species"].value_counts().sort_index()

species_counts.plot(kind="bar")

plt.xlabel("Species")
plt.ylabel("Number of observations")
plt.title("Number of Flowers by Species")
plt.xticks(rotation=0)
plt.show()
```

The bar chart shows that the dataset is balanced: each of the three Iris
species has the same number of observations.
